pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
> 📊 **Strand 4 — Handling Data**
Collecting, organising, presenting and interpreting information to make good decisions.

> 🎯 **Content standard** (B8.4.2)
- B8.4.2.1 — Identify the sample space for a probability experiment involving two independent events and express the probabilities of given events as fractions, decimals, percentages and/or ratios to solve problems.

> 🎯 **In this chapter you will learn to:**
- perform probability experiments with replacement and list sample spaces
- recognise independent events
- use tables and tree diagrams to find probabilities of combined events
- express probabilities as fractions, decimals, percentages and ratios

pages.title: Experiments with two independent events
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Perform a probability experiment involving two independent events, such as drawing coloured bottle tops from a bag with replacement, and list the elements of the sample space.
Curriculum indicator B8.4.2.1.1
> 🔑 **Key idea: Independent events** — Two events are **independent** if the outcome of one does **not affect** the outcome of the other. Picking an object, **replacing it**, and picking again gives independent trials, because the bag is the same each time.
## ✏️ Example 15.1
Emmanuel picks one bottle top from a bag containing 3 red (R), 2 green (G) and 1 pink (P) bottle top, notes its colour and replaces it. He does this three times.
a) List the sample space for one pick and for three picks. b) What is the probability of picking a red bottle top on any pick?
**Solution**
a) One pick: **{R, G, P}**. Three picks — every combination of three colours (3 × 3 × 3 = 27 outcomes):
{RRR, RRG, RRP, RGR, RGG, RGP, RPR, RPG, RPP, GRR, GRG, GRP, GGR, GGG, GGP, GPR, GPG, GPP, PRR, PRG, PRP, PGR, PGG, PGP, PPR, PPG, PPP}
b) Because the top is replaced, the bag always has 3 red out of 6: **P(R) =** [[3/6]] **=** [[1/2]] on every pick. (Note that the 27 colour patterns are not equally likely, because there are more red tops than pink ones.)

pages.title: Example 15.2
pages.body:
## ✏️ Example 15.2
Consider (a) throwing a fair six-sided die and (b) tossing a fair coin.
i) What is the sample space for (a) and for (b)? ii) Does the result of (a) affect (b)? iii) Find P(even number) and P(head). iv) What is the relationship between the two events?
**Solution**
i) (a) {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}; (b) {H, T}. Together:
|  | **1** | **2** | **3** | **4** | **5** | **6** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| H | (1, H) | (2, H) | (3, H) | (4, H) | (5, H) | (6, H) |
| T | (1, T) | (2, T) | (3, T) | (4, T) | (5, T) | (6, T) |
ii) **No** — the coin does not "know" what the die showed.
iii) P(even) = [[3/6]] = [[1/2]]; P(head) = [[1/2]].
iv) They are **independent events**. The probability that both happen, P(even and head), is [[3/12]] = [[1/4]] = [[1/2]] × [[1/2]].
## ✏️ Example 15.3
Ampofo walks to school daily and Serwa travels to school by bus daily. a) Does Ampofo's event affect Serwa's? b) Can the two events occur together?
**Solution**
a) **No** — how Ampofo travels has no effect on Serwa's bus. The events are independent.
b) **Yes** — both happen every school day at the same time.
> 🔑 **Key idea: Multiplication rule** — For independent events A and B: **P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)**.
> ✏️ **Practice:** Exercise 15.1, at the end of section 15.2, covers this section too. Tap **Quick check** to try its questions.

pages.title: Tree diagrams
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Express the probabilities of the events as fractions, decimals, percentages and/or ratios, e.g. using a tree diagram, table or other graphic organiser.
Curriculum indicator B8.4.2.1.2
> 🔑 **Key idea: Tree diagram** — A **tree diagram** shows each trial as a set of branches. Write the probability on each branch. The probabilities on the branches from one point add up to 1. **Multiply along** a path to find the probability of that combined outcome; **add** the results of paths that give the event you want.
## ✏️ Example 15.4
The spinner has four equal sectors: one marked W (win) and three marked L (lose). It is spun twice.
[[fig:m8-f53]]
a) Identify the sample space. b) Find P(W) and P(L) for one spin. c) Draw a tree diagram. d) Express the probabilities of the outcomes as fractions, decimals, percentages and ratios.
**Solution**
a) Sample space for two spins: **{WW, WL, LW, LL}**
b) P(W) = [[1/4]]; P(L) = [[3/4]]
c)
[[fig:m8-f54]]
Figure 15.1: Tree diagram for two spins
d)
| **Outcome** | **Fraction** | **Decimal** | **Percentage** | **Ratio (outcome : all)** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| WW | [[1/16]] | 0.0625 | 6.25% | 1 : 16 |
| WL | [[3/16]] | 0.1875 | 18.75% | 3 : 16 |
| LW | [[3/16]] | 0.1875 | 18.75% | 3 : 16 |
| LL | [[9/16]] | 0.5625 | 56.25% | 9 : 16 |
| Total | 1 | 1 | 100% |  |
P(at least one win) = [[1/16]] + [[3/16]] + [[3/16]] = [[7/16]] (or 1 − [[9/16]]).

pages.title: Example 15.5
pages.body:
## ✏️ Example 15.5
A box contains 3 blue pens and 4 pink pens. A pen is taken, its colour noted and it is replaced. A second pen is then taken. a) What is the sample space? b) Draw a tree diagram and find the probability of getting one pen of each colour.
**Solution**
a) {BB, BP, PB, PP}
b)
[[fig:m8-f55]]
Figure 15.2: Picking two pens with replacement
P(one of each) = P(BP) + P(PB) = [[12/49]] + [[12/49]] = [[24/49]] ≈ 0.49 ≈ 49%.
## ✏️ Example 15.6
A die is thrown at most three times. If a 6 is scored, the game stops. a) Draw a probability tree diagram. b) Explain why some branches "disappear". c) Find the probability of scoring a 6 at some point.
**Solution**
a)
[[fig:m8-f56]]
Figure 15.3: The game stops as soon as a 6 appears
b) Once a 6 is thrown the game ends, so there are no further throws on those branches.
c) P(6 on 1st) = [[1/6]]; P(6 on 2nd) = [[5/6]] × [[1/6]] = [[5/36]]; P(6 on 3rd) = [[5/6]] × [[5/6]] × [[1/6]] = [[25/216]].
P(a 6 at some point) = [[36/216]] + [[30/216]] + [[25/216]] = [[91/216]] ≈ 0.42
(Check: P(no 6 in three throws) = [[125/216]], and [[91/216]] + [[125/216]] = 1 ✓.)

pages.title: Exercise 15.1
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Exercise 15.1** — try these on paper or in your head, then tap **Quick check** to see the answers.
1. A coin is tossed twice. List the sample space and find the probability of: a) two heads b) one head and one tail c) at least one tail.
2. Two fair dice are thrown. Use a 6 × 6 table to find the probability that: a) the total is 7 b) both show the same number c) the total is more than 9.
3. A bag contains 5 red and 3 white balls. A ball is picked and replaced, then a second ball is picked. Draw a tree diagram and find: a) P(both red) b) P(both the same colour) c) P(at least one white). Give each as a fraction and a percentage.
4. The probability that Kofi is late for school on any day is 0.2. Find the probability that on two days: a) he is late on both days b) he is late on exactly one day.

pages.title: Chapter 15 summary
pages.body:
- Independent events do not affect each other; picking with replacement gives independent trials.
- P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) for independent events.
- Tree diagrams: multiply along branches; add the paths you need. Branch probabilities from a point add to 1.

questions.q: A fair coin is tossed and a spinner numbered 1–4 is spun. List the sample space and find P(head and an even number).
The probability that it rains on a given day is 0.3. Find the probability that it rains on neither of two days.
A bag has 2 yellow and 6 black beads. Two beads are picked with replacement. Find the probability of picking a yellow then a black bead, as a decimal and a percentage.
Explain why the events "picking a card from a pack" and "picking another card without replacing the first" are **not** independent.

parts.a: Without replacement, the pack has changed for the second pick, so the first result affects the second.
